description: We are 404: Rover Found, a Manila team in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are taking on the Moon and Mars discarded equipment storytelling challenge. With our web development and coding ready, we need teammates skilled in storytelling, writing, graphic design, and UI/UX to build the visuals and narratives with us.
summary: Echoes of Exploration: The NASA Signal Archive is an educational browser game for anyone interested in space exploration. Players guide UNIT-7, a fictional archival robot, across the Moon, Mars, and deep space to recover stories and records about 23 NASA hardware sites. The game also includes a catalog of 31 missions. Its dramatized stories and simplified gameplay are clearly distinguished from real, sourced mission facts.
details:
Echoes of Exploration: The NASA Signal Archive

What it does and how it works:

Players guide UNIT-7, a fictional archival robot, across the Moon (8 sites), Mars (9 sites), and Deep Space (6 sites) to recover 23 real NASA hardware records ("echoes") alongside a 31-mission catalog. Each site pairs exploration with one of five 60 Hz physics minigames (powered descent, rover traverse, laser/DSN signal lock, rotorcraft flight, or flyby imaging) or two science tasks (Viking soil ambiguity and Voyager 1 RTG power budgeting), unlocking verified mission summaries, coordinates, NASA photographs, and source links. All data ships locally with zero runtime API calls, and progress saves in browser localStorage.

Benefits and intended impact:

Designed for ages 10-13 and general learners, the game turns spacecraft engineering constraints into interactive intuition—helping players see abandoned hardware as enduring scientific infrastructure and heritage, while separating dramatized framing from verified NASA, JPL, NSSDCA, ILRS, and PDS records.

Tools, languages, and software:

Built with TypeScript, HTML5/CSS3, Phaser 3.90, Zod 3.24, Vite 6.1, Node.js (tsx), Python asset helpers, procedural Web Audio API sound synthesis, procedural pixel art, NASA Moon/Mars Trek maps, credited NASA Image Library photos, the Silkscreen font (SIL Open Font License 1.1), GitHub, and Vercel, tested on team PCs and smartphones. AI coding tools (Anthropic Claude and Google DeepMind Gemini/Antigravity) assisted with code, procedural art/audio, and data formatting; standalone generated illustrations carry SI-GENERATED ILLUSTRATION watermarks, no NASA insignias are used, and all facts and code were human-verified on 2026-11-14.

Creativity and key considerations:

Instead of one generic quiz, each minigame mirrors its spacecraft's real physics in a lightweight, offline-ready static app. Our team prioritized scientific citation accuracy, zero NASA endorsement, child privacy (no accounts, cookies, or tracking), mobile/desktop controls, and accessibility (text scaling, high contrast, reduced motion, captions, and optional challenge skip).
